disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by at least one fully syndromal manic episode lasting at least a week (or requiring hospitalization), often with marked impairment in social or occupational functioning. During severe manic episodes, mood-congruent or mood-incongruent psychotic features such as delusions or hallucinations can emerge, typically resolving as the mood episode remits. The course is usually recurrent, with episodes of mania and often depression separated by periods of relative euthymia, though some individuals have rapid cycling or chronic symptoms. It is distinguished from schizoaffective and primary psychotic disorders by the temporal relationship between psychosis and mood episodes and by the presence of clear-cut manic symptomatology.

narrative.stressor: In the months leading up to his episode, Roberto was promoted to lead a high-profile project integrating generative art into a major client’s platform, with an aggressive launch timeline that coincided with onboarding new team members and a corporate reorganization. Wanting to prove himself, he began extending his usual meticulous planning into increasingly ambitious goals, taking on additional side collaborations and late-night hackathons on top of his regular workload. Over roughly three months, his work-life balance eroded, and his normally disciplined routines around finances, exercise, and hiking were gradually replaced by a single-minded focus on shipping a "revolutionary" product, leading to escalating conflicts with colleagues and missed technical requirements that threatened the project. The situation became clinically significant when his spouse and manager noticed he was making risky unilateral decisions about architecture and contracts, insisting he had a "unique vision" others could not understand, and he ultimately agreed to psychiatric evaluation after HR intervened following several disruptive episodes at work and at a client pitch meeting.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m convinced I’ve figured out something so big in my work and art that normal rules and other people’s concerns just don’t apply to me right now.”

narrative.stressor: Dolores entered a particularly unstable period in her freelance work when two longstanding illustration contracts ended unexpectedly and an anticipated adjunct course was cancelled for low enrollment. Already prone to overcommitment, she reacted by saying yes to every new project offer, expanding her workload beyond what she could realistically manage, while also worrying about her irregular income and overdue taxes. Over the next three months, her previously comforting routines around gardening, walking, and museum visits were increasingly displaced by frantic efforts to "fix" her financial situation through ambitious new commissions and speculative proposals, straining her organization and leading to late payments and confused interactions with clients. Her sister and a close neighbor encouraged her to seek help after they noticed she was talking rapidly about improbable financial opportunities, neglecting basic paperwork, and insisting she had discovered a "sure way" to secure her retirement, prompting her to present for psychiatric care when she realized her money management and work commitments were spiraling out of control.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep taking on more and more projects and plans at once, and I can’t seem to slow myself down even though everything in my life is starting to fall apart.”

narrative.stressor: Allen’s episode emerged after a year marked by his own increasing joint pain and fatigue, coupled with his wife’s new diagnosis of a chronic cardiac condition that required frequent appointments and lifestyle changes. As he took on more caregiving tasks while trying to push forward with an ambitious "legacy" exhibition at the community center, his usual reflective pace gave way to a growing sense of urgency about completing his life’s work and preserving his creative vision. Over about three months, his days became dominated by elaborate art-related plans and late-night projects, with mounting tension at home as he diverted time and money from household needs toward impulsive purchases for the exhibition and made unusual claims about the historical importance of his work. His adult daughter and a longtime friend from the senior hiking club ultimately brought him to psychiatric care after he began speaking as if his art was being guided by unseen forces and showed increasing difficulty attending to his wife’s medical routines, leading them to worry that something more serious than stress or aging was happening.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I know people think it sounds strange, but I’m certain there are forces directing my art and that this exhibit has a special destiny, no matter what anyone says.”
